COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Panel‐data instrumental‐variables (IV) regression, implemented as a two-stage least squares (2SLS) event-study/DID hybrid (“tax-reform IV”).  

Rationale  
a. The outcome (log taxable income or log broad income) is continuous.  
b. The causal regressor of interest—the net-of-tax rate 1–τ_it—is mechanically endogenous because it depends on the taxpayer’s own income (reverse causality) and unobservables that affect both taxable income and deductions.  
c. Large, discrete federal and state reforms generate plausibly exogenous variation in statutory marginal rates that differs across taxpayers depending on their 1979 (or 1984) position in the income distribution.  
d. A standard solution is to build a “simulated” or “predicted” marginal tax rate that is a function only of the statutory schedule and a pre-determined (base-year) income. This instrument varies by individual and year but is uncorrelated with current-year income shocks, satisfying the exclusion restriction under the usual assumptions.  
e. The panel structure plus individual fixed effects purge permanent unobserved heterogeneity; year fixed effects absorb aggregate shocks.  

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
Treated = facing a larger change in the net-of-tax rate (Δlog(1–τ_it)) induced by the reforms. Operationally, the treatment intensity is the simulated change in the net-of-tax rate:  
Z_it ≡ log(1–τ̂_it) – log(1–τ̂_i,1979)  
where τ̂_it is the marginal rate that taxpayer i would face in year t if her real income stayed fixed at its 1979 level but the statutory schedules (federal + state) of year t applied.

Control group  
Taxpayers whose simulated net-of-tax rate changed little (e.g., those in the middle of the income distribution during ERTA and low-income families during TRA86) function as implicit controls. Because the design is continuous-treatment IV, we do not drop them; rather, they supply identifying counterfactual trends.

Treatment timing / events  
Major events: ERTA phase-in 1982-84 and TRA86 implementation 1987-88, plus state reforms on their statutory enactment dates. The instrument turns on automatically in the relevant years for each individual.

Additional endogenous regressors for income-effect decomposition  
Virtual income (VI_it), defined as net-of-tax income if earnings were zero, captures the lump-sum shift in the budget set. We estimate  
log Y_it = β_s log(1–τ_it) + β_I log VI_it + controls + FE + ε_it  
and instrument both log(1–τ_it) and log VI_it with their simulated counterparts.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Relevance: Simulated marginal rates are strongly correlated with actual marginal rates.  
Plausible: statutory reforms were large; first stages in prior work show F‐statistics > 100.

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on fixed effects and covariates, simulated rates affect current income only through their effect on actual marginal rates and virtual income.  
Plausible: simulation freezes base-year income, so any remaining correlation with shocks would have to operate through reform-specific channels unrelated to taxes.

A3. Parallel trends / common shocks: Absent tax-rate changes, taxpayers with different base-year incomes would have followed similar growth paths after controlling for age, state, and year effects.  
Plausible but testable via pre-trend event-study graphs.

A4. No differential migration or selective attrition correlated with simulated tax changes.  
Plausible for short-run tax planning horizons; we will verify by checking state movers and drop extreme cases.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): One person’s statutory rate change does not directly affect another’s taxable income.  
Plausible at the individual level for most earners.

4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  

T1. Mean reversion / non-tax income shocks correlate with base-year income.  
Remedy: (i) use five-year average of 1977-79 income when classifying base-year position; (ii) include individual fixed effects; (iii) include flexible controls for age*year and state*year.

T2. Income shifting across forms (e.g., reclassifying wages as corporate income after TRA86) inflates elasticity of taxable income relative to real income.  
Remedy: run parallel regressions on broad income; compare elasticities; interpret divergence as evidence of avoidance responses vs real supply.

T3. Concurrent policy shocks (EITC expansion, unemployment shocks) interact with income group.  
Remedy: (i) include controls for EITC eligibility × year dummies; (ii) limit sample to incomes above EITC plateau for robustness; (iii) control for state-year unemployment rates.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Load required packages
library(data.table)      # fast data handling
library(fixest)          # high-performance panel IV
library(ggplot2)

#----------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
#----------------------------------------------------
# Main tax panel (combined federal & state variables)
tax <- fread("nber_taxpanel_1979_1990.csv")  # ~46k obs/yr

#----------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
#----------------------------------------------------
# Drop excluded observations
tax <- tax[base_broad_income_1979 >= 10000 & marital_change == 0]

# Create panel identifiers
tax[, id := .GRP, by = ssn]               # individual id
setorder(tax, id, year)

# Compute outcomes
tax[, log_tax_inc  := log(taxable_income)]
tax[, log_broad    := log(broad_income)]

# Actual marginal tax rate (federal + state)
tax[, log_net_of_tax := log(1 - mtr_combined)]

# Virtual income (after-tax income at zero earnings)
tax[, log_VI := log(virtual_income)]

#----------------------------------------------------
# 3. Instruments: simulated MTR & VI
#----------------------------------------------------
# For each person, grab base-year real income (1979 $)
tax[, base_inc := first(broad_income[year == 1979]), by = id]

# Merge pre-computed simulated schedules (one row per id-year)
sim <- fread("simulated_mtr_vi.csv")     # contains id, year, sim_mtr, sim_VI
tax  <- merge(tax, sim, by = c("id","year"))

tax[, z_log_net := log(1 - sim_mtr)]
tax[, z_log_VI  := log(sim_VI)]

#----------------------------------------------------
# 4. Main 2SLS specification
# (elasticity of taxable income)
#----------------------------------------------------
spec1 <- feols(log_tax_inc ~ log_net_of_tax + log_VI | id + year | 
               (log_net_of_tax = z_log_net, log_VI = z_log_VI), data = tax, 
               cluster = ~id)

summary(spec1)

#----------------------------------------------------
# 5. Elasticity heterogeneity by income quartile
#----------------------------------------------------
tax[, quartile := cut(base_inc, quantile(base_inc, probs = 0:4/4), 
                     include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)]

spec_q <- feols(log_tax_inc ~ log_net_of_tax + log_VI | id + year |
                (log_net_of_tax = z_log_net, log_VI = z_log_VI),
                data = tax, by = ~ quartile, cluster = ~id)

etable(spec_q, tex = FALSE)

#----------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: Outcome = LOG BROAD INCOME
#----------------------------------------------------
spec_broad <- feols(log_broad ~ log_net_of_tax + log_VI | id + year | 
                    (log_net_of_tax = z_log_net, log_VI = z_log_VI), data = tax, 
                    cluster = ~id)

summary(spec_broad)

#----------------------------------------------------
# 7. Event-study pre-trend graph (placebo)
#----------------------------------------------------
# Build stacked event-time relative to TRA86 (event year = 1987)
tax[, rel_year := year - 1987]

es <- feols(log_tax_inc ~ i(rel_year, treated_bigcut, ref = -1) + controls | id + year,
            data = tax[abs(rel_year) <= 5])

iplot(es, ci = TRUE) + theme_minimal()
```

6. Expected Results  

Direction: β_s > 0. A fall in the marginal tax rate (rise in the net-of-tax rate) should increase reported taxable income; hence log elasticity is positive.  

Magnitude: Prior U.S. estimates for the 1980s suggest an elasticity of taxable income (ETI) between 0.2 and 0.4 for the full sample, with higher elasticities (≈0.6-0.8) among the top 1%. For broad income, expect a much smaller elasticity (≈0.05-0.15), implying that most of the taxable-income response reflects avoidance/substitution rather than changes in real factor supply. β_I (income effect) is predicted to be small and negative (around −0.05), consistent with leisure being a normal good.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
C1: Relevance (F-stat > 10) ……………………………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion (simulated rates affect outcome only via MTR) … 0.7  
C3: Stable composition / no selective attrition ………………… 0.8  
C4: Parallel pre-trends (validated graphically) ………………… 0.9  
C5: No spillovers or general-equilibrium feedback …………… 0.8  

Overall average ≈ 0.84 → design is reasonably credible but still subject to the usual caveats about avoidance behavior and concurrent policy shocks.
